title: Black Wall Street, Ep. 1 — The Elevator
evidence_boundary: Survivor testimony of the documented 1921 Tulsa Race Massacre. The narrator and her family are fictional; every surrounding event follows the documented record. Spiritual framing is her perception and never blames victims.
desired_movement: From unaware comfort to witnessing how a lie, a newspaper, and a mob unmade a city - while the spirit of Greenwood stays unbroken.
grounding: Greenwood Avenue, the Drexel Building elevator, the Tulsa Tribune, the courthouse line, the Frisco tracks.
invitation: Follow all ten parts - one survivor telling the whole story, start to finish.
era_style: 1921 documentary, black and white with hand-tinted moments

scenes.text: They set this machine in front of me and asked what I remember. Child, I am one hundred and six years old. Memory is near all I own, and it don't sit quiet. Lean in close now. Let me tell you about the world we built.
scenes.query: 1920s archival film, 1920s Black main-street bustle, storefronts and hats

scenes.text: Greenwood. Thirty-five square blocks on the north side of Tulsa, Oklahoma. Ten thousand of us. White folks took to calling it Black Wall Street. We just called it ours.
scenes.query: 1920s archival film, crowds outside Black-owned businesses, Sir Jones style

scenes.text: We had the Stradford, finest colored-owned hotel in America. The Dreamland Theatre, seven hundred fifty seats and a piano that never slept. Doctors, lawyers, two newspapers of our own.
scenes.image_prompt: authentic 1921 documentary photograph, prosperous 1921 Black business district street, brick hotel with striped awnings, theater marquee, parked Model T cars, black and white silver gelatin print, fine film grain, period-correct 1920s clothing and architecture, dignified historical tone

scenes.text: A dollar came into Greenwood and stayed, passing hand to hand to hand before it ever left. That wasn't luck, sugar. That was a people agreeing on what they were worth.
scenes.query: 1920s archival film, church congregation pouring out, families in Sunday best

scenes.text: My daddy was Dr. Ambrose Freeman. Office up a narrow stair on Greenwood Avenue, his name painted gold on the glass. Mama was his nurse when she wasn't being my mother — which she'd tell you was the harder job.
scenes.image_prompt: authentic 1921 documentary photograph, frosted glass office door with gold leaf physician lettering, narrow wooden staircase, oil sconce light, black and white silver gelatin print, fine film grain, period-correct 1920s clothing and architecture, dignified historical tone

scenes.text: I was eight that spring. Sunday dresses, penny candy, patent-leather shoes. In the one photograph we saved, somebody tinted my ribbon pink by hand. I remember that ribbon better than some whole years.
scenes.image_prompt: hand-tinted 1921 photograph, Black family of three on a wooden porch in Sunday best, mother father and small daughter with pink hair ribbon, formal portrait, delicate watercolor tint over black and white silver print, vintage postcard style, soft muted colors

scenes.text: Daddy used to say Greenwood was a thought before it was a town. Imagination is the workshop, Opal. Everything out here got built twice — once inside somebody, once in the brick.
scenes.query: 1920s archival film, children playing in a dirt lot, jump rope, wagons

scenes.text: We had our own schools too. Booker T. Washington High stood up on that hill like it knew something. We were not waiting on anybody's permission to be somebody. We already were.
scenes.image_prompt: authentic 1921 documentary photograph, proud brick high school building on a rise, students on the front steps in the distance, morning light, black and white silver gelatin print, fine film grain, period-correct 1920s clothing and architecture, dignified historical tone

scenes.text: Monday, May thirtieth, 1921. Memorial Day. Flags all down Main Street, veterans marching, most stores shut. The parade was downtown — the white part of town — but a workday don't stop for everybody.
scenes.query: 1920s archival film, Memorial Day parade, flags, marching veterans, 1921

scenes.text: Dick Rowland was nineteen. Shined shoes on Main. Folks called him Diamond Dick. I knew his grin the way a child knows grown folks — by the kindness or the lack of it. His was kindness.
scenes.image_prompt: authentic 1921 documentary photograph, young Black man at a shoeshine stand on a busy main street, kind confident grin, customer shoe on the brass rest, black and white silver gelatin print, fine film grain, period-correct 1920s clothing and architecture, dignified historical tone

scenes.text: Jim Crow did its arithmetic on him daily. The only washroom a colored man could use downtown sat at the top of the Drexel Building. To reach it, you rode the elevator. That is all that boy was doing.
scenes.image_prompt: authentic 1921 documentary photograph, 1921 downtown office building, stone facade and revolving door, pedestrians in straw boaters, black and white silver gelatin print, fine film grain, period-correct 1920s clothing and architecture, dignified historical tone

scenes.text: The elevator girl was Sarah Page, seventeen, white, working her shift same as any Monday. Two young people in a box of brass and cable. History has squeezed into smaller rooms than that, child. Not many.
scenes.query: 1920s archival film, downtown Tulsa street, streetcars and awnings

scenes.text: The car lurched. He stumbled. His hand caught her arm the way you would catch anybody's arm. She hollered. He ran — because a colored boy in 1921 knew exactly what a holler could cost him.
scenes.image_prompt: authentic 1921 documentary photograph, ornate brass scissor-gate elevator interior, operator stool and control lever, empty, overhead lamp, black and white silver gelatin print, fine film grain, period-correct 1920s clothing and architecture, dignified historical tone

scenes.text: A clerk from the store next door heard the scream, saw a Black boy running, and let his imagination finish the story. Fear writes fast, child. Faster than truth can lace its shoes.
scenes.image_prompt: authentic 1921 documentary photograph, 1921 clothing store display window, suited mannequins, street reflections in the glass, black and white silver gelatin print, fine film grain, period-correct 1920s clothing and architecture, dignified historical tone

scenes.text: Now here is what nobody led with: the police who talked to Sarah Page didn't smell much fire in it. No charge she would swear to. The detectives shrugged. On any honest day, that is where it ends.
scenes.query: 1920s archival film, police station exterior, officers on steps

scenes.text: That night we slept easy under our own roofs, in the town we built twice. I have spent a hundred years learning how precious an easy sleep is, child. That was the last one for a long while.
scenes.image_prompt: hand-tinted 1921 photograph, rooftops of a small prosperous district at dusk, chimneys and a church steeple, warm amber sky, delicate watercolor tint over black and white silver print, vintage postcard style, soft muted colors
scenes.symbol_query: record needle travels across spinning vinyl beside old photographs soft window light

scenes.text: Tuesday morning, May thirty-first, they arrested Dick anyway, quiet, and set him in the courthouse jail. Sheriff Willard McCullough held the keys. Remember his name. Goodness wore every color that week.
scenes.image_prompt: authentic 1921 documentary photograph, courthouse jail corridor, iron bars, single wooden chair, one shaft of window light, black and white silver gelatin print, fine film grain, period-correct 1920s clothing and architecture, dignified historical tone

scenes.text: Greenwood didn't know one thing about it yet. Supper smells drifting, the Dreamland piano warming up, men sweeping their own storefronts. We were rich in the way that counts — we belonged to each other.
scenes.query: 1920s archival film, Greenwood evening street life, storefront lamps

scenes.text: But downtown, an afternoon paper needed selling. The Tulsa Tribune. And there is no cheaper fuel on God's green earth than a white woman's scream and a Black man's name.
scenes.image_prompt: authentic 1921 documentary photograph, 1921 newspaper office building, tall windows, newsprint rolls stacked at the loading dock, delivery truck, black and white silver gelatin print, fine film grain, period-correct 1920s clothing and architecture, dignified historical tone

scenes.text: They set it in type: NAB NEGRO FOR ATTACKING GIRL IN AN ELEVATOR. Eight words, most of them seasoning on a story that had no meat. A match, child, dipped in ink.
scenes.image_prompt: authentic 1921 documentary photograph, linotype typesetting machine closeup in a print shop, rows of metal type gleaming, operator hands at the keys, black and white silver gelatin print, fine film grain, period-correct 1920s clothing and architecture, dignified historical tone

scenes.text: And deeper in that paper, folks swore, an invitation to a lynching, printed plain. Go look for it today. That page is torn out of every archive by somebody's careful hand. Paper burns, baby. Witness don't.
scenes.query: 1920s archival film, press room, rolls thundering through the press

scenes.text: A little after three, the Tribune hit the street. Newsboys hollering that headline on every corner downtown. Folks said you could stand on our side of the tracks and feel it coming. Like weather.
scenes.query: 1920s archival film, newsboys hawking papers on a corner

scenes.text: By suppertime, white Tulsa had chewed that story down to one word: rope. A mob had lynched a white boy in this same town not a year before, and the law just watched. Everybody knew the recipe worked.
scenes.image_prompt: authentic 1921 documentary photograph, cluster of white men in straw boaters and fedoras reading a newspaper together on a sidewalk, stern faces, black and white silver gelatin print, fine film grain, period-correct 1920s clothing and architecture, dignified historical tone

scenes.text: By seven-thirty they were collecting outside the courthouse. Hundreds, then more. McCullough barred the doors, killed the elevator, put riflemen on the stairs. The mob asked for Dick Rowland. The sheriff said no.
scenes.query: 1920s archival film, courthouse exterior, crowd thickening at dusk

scenes.text: Down on Greenwood, men who had worn this country's uniform in France set down their suppers and stood up. If the law could not hold that line, they would. Not rage, child. Arithmetic. They knew what mobs do.
scenes.image_prompt: authentic 1921 documentary photograph, formal studio portrait of Black World War One soldiers in uniform, campaign hats, dignified upright posture, black and white silver gelatin print, fine film grain, period-correct 1920s clothing and architecture, dignified historical tone

scenes.text: Daddy locked the office early. Mama held my hand too tight, and the air had changed — you could taste tomorrow in it, like copper. Next time I'll tell you how one gun went off and the whole world tore its shirt.
scenes.query: 1920s archival film, dark street, lamplight, two figures walking

scenes.text: This is Black Wall Street, part one of ten. I'm telling the whole story, child — every part of it, right here on this channel. Go on and find part two. The night I lost my easy sleep is waiting on you.
